name: Low-dose finasteride microdosing
lead: Low-dose finasteride microdosing is a practice in which men with pattern hair loss take finasteride in amounts below the 1 mg daily dose approved for hair loss, usually hoping to keep hair benefits while lowering the chance of sexual or mood side effects. Finasteride is a prescription 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor sold as Propecia (1 mg) for hair loss and Proscar (5 mg) for benign prostatic hyperplasia.[1]

Encyclopedic sources report that a 0.2 mg daily dose achieved near-maximal reduction of circulating DHT, 68.6 percent, compared with 72.2 percent at 5 mg.[1] No large randomized trials establishing the hair efficacy or side-effect rates of lower-than-approved doses were identified for this article.
The practice is not a labelled use, and people considering it generally discuss it with prescribers.

paras: Microdosing here refers to using less than the labelled amount, such as fractions of a tablet. This article does not give dosing instructions. Finasteride was approved by the FDA in 1992 for prostate enlargement and in 1997 at 1 mg for male pattern hair loss.[1]

At 5 mg per day, circulating DHT falls about 65 to 70 percent and prostate DHT 80 to 90 percent; finasteride mainly inhibits type II and III 5-alpha-reductase.[1] A 0.2 mg daily dose reportedly produced a 68.6 percent DHT reduction, close to the 72.2 percent at 5 mg.[1] Finasteride also affects neurosteroids such as allopregnanolone.[1]

Proponents reason that since DHT suppression plateaus at low doses, smaller amounts may preserve most benefit while reducing dose-related adverse effects. Sources report sexual side effects including decreased libido and erectile dysfunction, and a 2017 review of about 12,000 patients found persistent erectile dysfunction in 1.4 percent.[1] Whether lower doses reduce these risks has not been established in the sources reviewed.

The FDA updated labelling in 2012 to include persistent sexual effects, and in 2025 the European Medicines Agency confirmed that suicidal thoughts can occur with finasteride, mostly at the 1 mg dose.[1]

No studies found directly comparing microdoses of finasteride with the approved dose for hair outcomes or side effects. Related pharmacology data on DHT suppression at 0.2 mg is reported in encyclopedic summaries.[1]

timeline.event: FDA approves finasteride 5 mg (Proscar) for BPH.[1]
FDA approves 1 mg (Propecia) for male pattern hair loss.[1]
FDA label update on persistent sexual effects.[1]
EMA confirms suicidal thoughts as a possible side effect.[1]

card.summary: Taking below-label finasteride to cut side effects; DHT data are suggestive but trials on lower doses are lacking.
card.note: Off-label; finasteride carries label warnings on sexual and mood effects.

quick.overview:
Microdosing means using less finasteride than the labelled 1 mg hair-loss dose, in hope of lowering side effects while keeping hair benefits.

Pharmacology reports show DHT suppression is near-maximal at low doses, but trials comparing hair results and side effects across doses were not found.
quick.mechanism: Finasteride blocks type II and III 5-alpha-reductase, reducing DHT. A reported 0.2 mg dose lowered DHT 68.6 percent versus 72.2 percent at 5 mg.
quick.risks: Label warnings cover sexual dysfunction, depression and suicidal thoughts; the EMA confirmed suicidal thoughts in 2025. It is Rx-only and contraindicated in pregnancy. Whether lower doses reduce risk is unproven.
